title: Section 4
context: A marine biology lecturer is giving a talk about how damaged coral reefs can be restored.

audio.t: Section 4. You will hear a lecturer talking to a group of students about the restoration of coral reefs.
Good morning, everyone. Today I'd like to talk about something hopeful for a change: how we can help damaged coral reefs recover.
Let's start with why reefs matter so much. If you look at my first slide, you'll see that reefs cover less than ten per cent of the ocean floor.
Sorry, that's a mistake on the slide. The correct figure is less than one per cent. I'll fix it before I upload the slides.
Even so, that tiny area supports about a quarter of all marine species, which is an extraordinary proportion.
The best known threat is coral bleaching. It happens when the water becomes too warm, and the coral loses the colourful algae living inside it.
A bleached reef isn't necessarily dead, but it's weak, and repeated bleaching can destroy it. That's where restoration comes in.
The first technique is called coral gardening. Small fragments of healthy coral are collected, often pieces that have broken off naturally in storms.
These fragments are then hung on frames in underwater nurseries, where they can grow in calm, protected conditions.
When the fragments are ready, divers attach them to the damaged reef. Early projects used a strong glue called epoxy for this.
However, most teams have now switched to marine cement. It's cheaper, and it doesn't release chemicals into the water.
The species most often used is staghorn coral, because it grows so quickly. Older studies suggested it grew about ten centimetres a year.
But recent measurements show that in good conditions it can reach as much as fifteen centimetres a year.
How long do the fragments stay in the nursery? In the first trials it was only about four months, but that proved too short.
Most projects now wait around six months, so the pieces are big enough to survive when they're moved.
And what about survival? You'll sometimes read that ninety per cent of transplanted fragments survive. That's true in a few sheltered bays.
Across all the projects I've reviewed, though, the average is about seventy per cent, which is still very encouraging.
The second approach looks to the future. Scientists are selecting and breeding corals that can tolerate higher temperatures.
They find colonies that survived a hot summer without bleaching and use them as parents. Their offspring then seem to cope better with warm water.
Some researchers call this assisted evolution, and it's still at an early stage, but the first results are promising.
The third method uses artificial structures. One well known design is called Biorock. It's a steel frame placed on the sea bed.
A weak electric current passes through the frame, and minerals from the seawater gradually build up on the steel. Coral fragments attached to it tend to grow much faster.
Of course, none of this works without the people who live near the reef.
In several countries, local fishermen have been trained to monitor the reefs and report any damage. They know the area better than anyone.
They are also paid for the work, which gives them a good reason to protect the reef rather than fish in it unsustainably.
To sum up, restoration can't replace the protection of healthy reefs, and it can't stop the oceans warming.
But it does buy precious time, and it shows that people can repair some of the damage we have caused. Thank you, and now I'll take your questions.

blocks.instructions: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

questions.q: Coral reefs cover less than ______% of the ocean floor.
questions.explain: Slide ghi 10% nhưng giảng viên sửa ngay: "The correct figure is less than one per cent."

questions.q: They support about a quarter of all marine ______.
questions.explain: "That tiny area supports about a quarter of all marine species."

questions.q: Coral gardening: fragments are grown in underwater ______.
questions.explain: "These fragments are then hung on frames in underwater nurseries."

questions.q: Fragments are now attached to the reef using marine ______.
questions.explain: Dự án đầu dùng keo epoxy, nhưng "most teams have now switched to marine cement" vì rẻ hơn và không thải hóa chất.

questions.q: Staghorn coral can grow up to ______ cm a year.
questions.explain: Nghiên cứu cũ nói 10 cm, nhưng số đo mới cho thấy "as much as fifteen centimetres a year".

questions.q: Fragments now stay in the nursery for about ______ months.
questions.explain: Thử nghiệm đầu chỉ 4 tháng nhưng quá ngắn; nay "Most projects now wait around six months".

questions.q: The average survival rate of transplanted fragments is about ______%.
questions.explain: 90% chỉ đúng ở vài vịnh kín gió; "the average is about seventy per cent".

questions.q: Scientists are breeding corals that can tolerate higher ______.
questions.explain: "Selecting and breeding corals that can tolerate higher temperatures."

questions.q: Biorock structures are steel frames with a weak ______ current passing through them.
questions.explain: "A weak electric current passes through the frame" giúp khoáng chất bám vào thép.

questions.q: Local ______ are trained to monitor the reefs.
questions.explain: "Local fishermen have been trained to monitor the reefs and report any damage."
